title: Longer out than in
hook: slow breathing with a longer exhale tends to calm the body, a finding repeated in many lab studies

segments.voice: Yesterday you only watched. No fixing, no counting, just noticing the breath come and go. Your line was it breathes. Did you catch it breathing on its own, somewhere in the day? Day ninety-eight.

Think about the last time you were really upset. A near miss on the highway. A message that made your face go hot. What did your breath do? Most people find it went short and high, up in the chest, quick in and quick out. And now think about what you do without being taught when the danger passes. You let out a long breath. Whew. Nobody gives lessons in whew. Every culture seems to have some version of it. It's as if the body already knows something about the out-breath. Today we slow it down on purpose. Today: longer out than in.

Here's the simple version of what's going on. Your heart doesn't beat at one steady speed. When you breathe in, it tends to speed up a little. When you breathe out, it tends to slow down a little. You can feel this yourself if you hold two fingers on your wrist and breathe slowly. The slowing on the out-breath is linked to the vagus nerve, a long nerve that runs from the brain down through the chest and belly, and is part of the body's rest-and-digest system. So if you make the out-breath longer than the in-breath, you spend more of each minute in the slowing half. That's the idea. And it isn't only an idea. Researchers have put people in labs, slowed their breathing to around six breaths a minute, often with a longer exhale, and measured heart rate, blood pressure, and how calm people say they feel. Many of these studies find a calming effect. Most are small, and they don't all agree on the details, so the honest word is tends. A longer exhale tends to calm the body. It isn't a cure, and it won't fix what upset you. But it can turn the volume down enough for you to think. The old traditions noticed the breath long before any lab. Yoga teachers in India have taught slow exhales for centuries, and singers, swimmers and flute players all learn to make an out-breath last. The lab gives us a way to test what the whew already knew.
screen: `IN SPEEDS UP, OUT SLOWS DOWN.` · `THE VAGUS NERVE.` · `SIX BREATHS A MINUTE, IN THE LAB.` · `IT TENDS TO CALM.` · then, large: `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: in for four, out for six. Sit so your back is easy and your shoulders can drop. Breathe in through your nose, slowly, counting one, two, three, four. Then let it out, through your nose or softly through your lips, one, two, three, four, five, six. No need to force it. If six feels like too much, try five, and let it grow. If you feel light-headed, go back to normal breathing for a while. Just keep the out a little longer than the in. The bell holds the time.
Longer out than in. A slow breath with a longer exhale, which tends to calm the body. Today's word.
Your line: longer out. Today, the next time your breath goes short and high, at a red light or a hard email, give it three breaths with a long exhale before you answer. Day ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Slow breathing with a longer exhale, often around six breaths a minute, is taught in yoga classes, therapy offices and stress-management courses, and is one of the most studied breathing patterns in the lab.

original.note: Sanskrit, from yoga's breath practice: the exhale, the breath let out.

trapdoor: what you thought: breathe slowly and you'll relax.
what it means: a longer out-breath spends more of each minute in the part of the breath where the heart slows.
what a scholar hears: the rise and fall of heart rate with the breath, called respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which many slow-breathing studies measure.

notes: Claims kept deliberately modest ('tends to calm', 'most are small'). A scientist should confirm the summary of the slow-breathing literature and the Zaccaro 2018 citation.
Vagus nerve described in lay terms as part of 'rest-and-digest'; confirm this simplification is acceptable.
Sanskrit रेचक (recaka) for exhalation, pronunciation RAY-chuh-kuh: confirm.
The claim that yoga teachers have taught slow exhales 'for centuries' rests on hatha yoga texts such as the Hatha Yoga Pradipika (c. 15th century): confirm the framing.
